outgoing.explanation: Reads Anderson's directory entry for what its "Boston" settlement attribution rests on.
The same conflation explains the American 1615-birth tradition and Anderson's Boston attribution.
The conflation reading depends on the 1636 Newgate apprentice being a distinct, younger man.

sources.alignmentNote: Anderson's entry is the object of this analysis. Its own reading as a coverage statement is carried in g13-colonial-record-coverage (G13-RI-000039).
sources.locator: p. 158, John Gurney entry: settlement "Boston, Braintree"; origin "Unknown."

finding.statement: Anderson's Great Migration Directory gives John Gurney's New England settlements as Boston and Braintree, but no Boston record names him. The attribution is most plausibly the same conflation that produced the American family tradition of an 1615 birth at Southwark: the 1636 runaway apprentice John Gurney - a distinct, younger man - was bound to John Newgate the feltmaker and lived in Newgate's Boston household, a servant's position that would generate neither a church admission nor a property record. A short unrecorded stay at Boston by the elder John before he appears at Weymouth in June 1641 remains possible; Boston lay under a day away and traded with Weymouth constantly. But transient lodging is invisible in principle, so the scenario can be neither tested nor used.
